PROTEST OF 
EAST KENTUCKY POWER COOPERATIVE, INC.  
 
Pursuant to Rule 211 of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure1 and the 
Commission’s August 3, 2026 “Combined Notice of Filings #1,” East Kentucky Power 
Cooperative, Inc. (“EKPC”)2 hereby protests the July 31, 2026 filing3 of PJM Interconnection, 
L.L.C. (“PJM”) proposing revisions to its Open Access Transmission Tariff (“Tariff”) and 
Reliability Assurance Agreement Among Load Serving Entities (“RAA”) to establish the 
Reliability Backstop Procurement (“RBP”). PJM proposes the RBP to be a one-time procurement 
of new capacity resources intended to address previously identified resource adequacy challenges 
that have arisen as a result of insufficient capacity commitments in the 2027/2028 and 2028/2029 
Reliability Pricing Model (“RPM”) Capacity Market Auctions (“RBP Proposal”).   EKPC shares 
the concern that PJM is attempting to address; however, this is not the right fix.  The PJM RBP 
Proposal is unjust and unreasonable, improperly expands the role of an Electric Distributor in PJM, 
and is inconsistent with the boundaries of federal and state jurisdiction.  Despite its claims to the 
contrary, PJM’s RBP Proposal also fails to address concerns raised by the Commission and the 
Governors of the 13 PJM states regarding the impacts of large loads, specifically ratepayer 
protection. Indeed, EKPC is significantly concerned about the potential cost shifting that could

I. 
Background 
A. RBP Overview 
As proposed by PJM, the RBP is a one-time capacity procurement targeting an Unforced 
Capacity (“UCAP”) shortfall identified in the 2027/2028 and 2028/2029 RPM Capacity Market 
Auctions. PJM claims that “[t]o mitigate the potential reliability risks associated with resource 
adequacy shortfalls, PJM is proposing this RBP as a supplementary mechanism to procure 
additional supply to meet the resource adequacy needs of the PJM Region.”4 PJM asserts that 
“[t]he RBP proposal is a just and reasonable means to address the influx of large loads while 
maintaining resource adequacy, reliability, and affordability in a manner that respects the divide 
between state and federal authorities and avoids disrupting existing commercial arrangements.”5 
Fundamentally, according to PJM, the RBP has the “goal of obtaining commitments of 
new RBP UCAP MW from eligible resources, called RBP Resources, for a fixed term of up to 15 
years, starting with the 2028/2029 Delivery Year and ending with the 2042/2043 Delivery Year.”6  
The RBP intends to accomplish this goal by conducting a one-time auction to procure new capacity 
equal to the identified “RBP Target.” The RBP Target is equal to the “Initial RBP Target,” which 
is the region-wide 2028/2029 Delivery Year reliability shortfall observed in the July 2026 Base 
Residual Auction (“BRA”) for Delivery Year 2028/2029, i.e., 6,831.3 MW UCAP, minus

the relevant state governor, Relevant Electric Retail Regulatory Authority (“RERRA”), and

RBP. 
Importantly, PJM is not proposing to match specific supply to specific demand.11 In other 
words, PJM is not utilizing a register or other means to ensure specific LSEs serving large loads 
throughout the 15-year duration are appropriately charged the costs associated with the

Nor is PJM applying any locational constraints in determining which resources to select 
for 15-year commitments.  PJM claims that “locational parameters based on today’s conditions 
would inevitably skew the results and lead to either over-procurement or under-procurement in 
given zones based on nothing more than speculation as to the state of the system ten and fifteen 
years from now.”13 As PJM asserts, “inclusion of a speculative 15-year forward locational capacity 
requirement at this point in time would simply ignore the role of PJM’s interconnection and 
planning process as the means to ensure deliverability of capacity resources to load throughout the 
PJM Region.”14 
According to PJM, the RBP is designed to attract new supplies of capacity.15 Under PJM’s 
proposal, resources procured through the RBP must demonstrate a high degree of certainty of 
achieving commercial operation within the next few years and be available to provide capacity 
until the end of a fixed, 15-year term.16 Sellers eligible to participate in the RBP, i.e., RBP 
Resources or Market Participants selling RBP UCAP MW of RBP Resources, must: “(1) meet 
collateral requirements prior to participating in the RBP; (2) support eligibility to provide capacity; 
(3) provide capacity; (4) cover penalties for any capacity shortfalls; and (5) bear responsibility for 
defaults.”17 Similarly, buyers, i.e., LSEs, must: “(1) meet collateral requirements immediately

The RBP will use a pay-as-bid clearing structure with a MW-weighted average levelized 
procurement cost cap of $555/MW-day UCAP, which is based on Point 1 of the Variable Resource 
Requirement (“VRR”) curve for the 2028/2029 BRA.19 Resources selected through the RBP are 
committed for a fixed 15-year term, commencing with the 2028/2029 Delivery Year and extending 
through the 2042/2043 Delivery Year.20 PJMSettlement acts as the counterparty to RBP 
commitments, and RBP Resources must offer as price takers ($0/MW-day) in RPM Capacity 
Market auctions. PJM proposes to commit resources in the RBP using a pay-as-bid approach, 
which PJM explains is more appropriate for a one-time backstop procurement than the single-
clear-price approach used in the RPM Capacity Market.21  
As proposed by PJM, cost allocation under the RBP flows first to Electric Distributor 
zones/areas based on Load Adjustments per RAA Schedule 8, then to LSEs based on state- or 
RERRA-determined RBP Obligations (“RBOs”). In the absence of reported RBOs, PJM’s backup 
methodology uses Daily Unforced Capacity Obligation ratios. Costs will be allocated to PJM zones 
based on their pro rata share of the procurement target and then allocated to utilities and other 
LSEs within the zones. As explained by PJM, it “is proposing to allocate daily RBP Charges to 
relevant Electric Distributor zones/areas, pro rata, based on the zone/area’s assigned share of the 
total, region-wide Final RBP Target MW, floored at zero,” incorporating certain Load

costs pursuant to RAA, Schedule 8.”26 Overall, PJM claims that its proposed cost allocation

PJM has also proposed to restrict an FRR entity’s use of bilateral contracts to satisfy its

A. The Stakeholder Process and Coalition RBP Proposal 
PJM claims that “the RBP reflects the input of stakeholders, as well as PJM’s judgment 
and analyses in shaping the specific means to implement the Principles document.”36 During the 
stakeholder process intended to consider options to address the identified capacity shortfall, PJM 
considered 13 proposals that were voted on June 30, 2026, through the Critical Issue Fast Path 
(“CIFP”) process. Of those proposals, only the Coalition RBP Proposal, discussed in more detail 
below, received the required two-thirds sector-weighted member support. The PJM Board, in its 
July 27, 2026 decisional letter, rejected this voluntary, stakeholder-supported proposal and instead 
directed PJM to file the mandatory procurement framework at issue here.37 PJM acknowledges

For the reasons explained herein, EKPC urges the Commission to reject the PJM RBP 
Proposal as unjust, unreasonable, and unduly discriminatory.44 EKPC also urges the Commission 
to clarify the revision proposed to FRR will not preclude the ability of any entity electing to utilize 
the FRR alternative in the future to satisfy its PJM capacity obligations to rely upon existing 
bilateral contracts in its long-standing supply portfolio.   
II. 
Protest 
PJM claims that the RBP is “a critical safety net designed to address current resource 
adequacy shortfalls.”45 EKPC shares PJM’s concern about resource adequacy and the reliability 
challenges facing the PJM region, and EKPC supports measures that maintain resource adequacy

43 The Coalition proposed a Large Load Registry maintained by PJM, through which the Large Load or its designated

to net appropriately to avoid double payment for overlapping capacity obligations.

and recognizes the urgency of PJM’s reliability concerns. But as filed, the PJM RBP Proposal will 
fail to achieve its objectives in a manner consistent with the requirements of the Federal Power 
Act (“FPA”). The PJM RBP Proposal assigns long-term costs and collateral obligations through a 
framework that lacks the specificity necessary to be just and reasonable. In particular, PJM’s RBP 
Proposal does not sufficiently identify the LSE responsible for causing the capacity shortage, 
ensure that any offsets or opt-outs follow the entity that secured them, or protect LSEs whose 
existing resource portfolios already support their expected load obligations from incurring 
additional costs. PJM’s RBP Proposal may attempt to address a legitimate reliability need. But 
simply attempting to address a legitimate need is not enough to make the RBP Proposal just and 
reasonable, especially where the resulting costs are not reasonably tied to cost causation, and the 
cost allocation and credit and collateral obligations are not knowable, hedgeable, or administrable. 
These uncertainties, in turn, will frustrate PJM’s stated purpose and serve to actually increase the 
default risk that has broader implications for the PJM region. That risk extends to entities like 
EKPC whose supply portfolio contains sufficient resources to serve the load underlying PJM’s 
forecast that was the basis for its calculation of the shortfall the RBP is attempting to address.46

and cost causation.”48  He also provides an analysis as to why the RBP’s cost-and-risk allocation

Moreover, the ambiguity PJM has introduced with respect to what qualifies as an existing resource

heavily on long-term, bilateral contracts.66 
The PJM RBP Proposal creates unmitigable financial and reliability risk for LSEs that 
prudently planned for their load or otherwise did not cause the residual RBP procurement need. It 
also creates a potential significant burden for those LSEs that may not have sufficiently planned 
and may have anticipated costs from RBP associated with only their contribution to the need. If 
the weight of the imposed burden causes defaults, that increases risk for the entire market. The 
financial and reliability risks and burdens imposed on all market participants will inhibit growth 
and ultimately discourage investment in the PJM region. Moreover, and most strikingly, the RBP 
Proposal also undermines the Administration’s and PJM state Governor’ ratepayer-protection 
objectives because it has the potential to shift large-load-driven costs to customers and LSEs that 
did not create the need for those costs. Indeed, the default allocation provision explicitly would 
assign costs to all LSEs in a zone/area without regard to whether those affected zones/aeras serve 
a new large load.  Therefore, the Commission should reject the RBP Proposal.

A. 
The PJM RBP Proposal is Not Just and Reasonable.  
a. PJM’s RBP Proposal is Unjust and Unreasonable Because the Resulting 
Rate Impact is Uncertain.  
Under section 205 of the FPA, rates must be “just and reasonable.”67 Section 205(c) of the 
FPA “requires rate filings to recite ‘the … practices … affecting such rates and charges.’” The 
Commission’s regulations also require rate schedules to set forth “clearly and specifically … the 
classifications, practices, rules and regulations affecting such rates, charges, classifications, 
services … ”68 The PJM RBP Proposal does not provide sufficiently bounded and causation-based 
inputs for determining which LSE is responsible for RBP charges. The PJM RBP Proposal does 
not explain how qualifying offsets or opt-outs follow the responsible LSE such that its allocation 
appropriately can be calibrated or reduced to zero. Nor does it make clear when collateral 
obligations attach. Relying on the Electric Distributor and RERRA to make determinations or 
otherwise effectuate downstream processes does not replace the need to ensure the appropriate 
wholesale entity is allocated the costs. Therefore, the cost allocation put forward as part of the PJM 
RBP Proposal fails to meet this standard, and is not just and reasonable.  
The Commission has rejected proposed cost allocations when the proposals, like the PJM 
RBP Proposal here, lack specificity or do not allow impacted customers to be able to estimate the 
cost impact. In California Power Exchange Corp., for example, the Commission rejected the cost 
allocation plan of the California Power Exchange Corporation (“PX”) for its Block-Forward 
Market because the plan “lack[ed] specificity with regard to items which will not be directly 
assigned” and “ha[d] not linked the allocation methodologies to particular costs to be allocated.”69

governance and cost-allocation principle. It recognizes that large loads may produce economic benefits 
and that PJM may need additional resources to serve them reliably. At the same time, it requires PJM to 
link, as directly as practicable, the incremental reliability consequences of serving those loads to the LSEs 
that supply them.

tenant might do, not to the rent due over the life of the lease. A landlord who demanded six 
months’ rent as a deposit on a twelve-month lease would be asked what damage he expected. That 
is approximately what the Credit Rate demands, measured against the gross value of the RBP 
commitment on PJM’s own derivation. Measured against the exposure the collateral actually 
secures, it demands considerably more. The filing does not identify the corresponding measured 
exposure. 
PART ONE — FRAMEWORK 
III.  THE ROLE OF COLLATERAL 
10. 
This section establishes the standards that govern collateral and margining in commercial and 
organized markets. Those standards are not matters of individual judgment. They are set out in 
published guidance issued by the Committee on Payments and Market Infrastructures of the Bank 
for International Settlements together with the International Organization of Securities 
Commissions, adopted by the Financial Stability Board as one of twelve key standards essential to 
financial stability, and, for the organized wholesale electric markets specifically, in the orders and 
credit policy of this Commission. PJM’s own Attachment Q is constructed on the same 
architecture. I set out those standards here so that the proposed RBP credit requirement can be 
measured against them in the sections that follow. 
11. 
Collateral secures replacement cost, not the contract. It is a risk instrument, not a revenue 
instrument. The governing international standard defines the exposure being secured as 
replacement-cost risk — “the risk of loss of unrealised gains on unsettled transactions with a 
counterparty,” where “the resulting exposure is the cost of replacing the original transaction at 
current market prices.” CPSS-IOSCO, Principles for Financial Market Infrastructures (April 2012) 
(“PFMI”) ¶ 2.5.

4 
 
12. 
Collateral is accordingly held “to cover current and potential future exposures.” PFMI ¶ 1.13. 
Principle 4 requires that credit exposures be effectively measured, monitored and managed, and 
Principle 6 requires that a margin system be “risk-based and regularly reviewed.” 
13. 
Price. Loss is contract price less replacement price. Because replacement price moves with the 
market, margin levels must be “commensurate with the risks and particular attributes of each 
product, portfolio, and market” the infrastructure serves. PFMI, Principle 6, Key Consideration 1. 
Exposure is therefore recalculated rather than fixed. 
14. 
Liquidation. The exposure period runs from default to replacement. PFMI Principle 6, Key 
Consideration 3 requires initial margin models “sufficient to cover its potential future exposure to 
participants in the interval between the last margin collection and the close out of positions 
following a participant default,” using “a conservative estimate of the time horizons for the 
effective hedging or close out of the particular types of products cleared.” The driver is the close-
out horizon, not the remaining term of the contract. 
15. 
Sizing therefore requires answering three questions: what position is being replaced, at what price, 
and over what period. That is the structure of PFMI Principle 6, and it is the structure of the 
Commission’s own credit policy, which identifies the function of collateral as preventing the 
socialization of a default across the membership. Policy Statement on Electric Creditworthiness, 
109 FERC ¶ 61,186, P 17 (2004); Credit Reforms in Organized Wholesale Electric Markets, Order 
No. 741-A, 134 FERC ¶ 61,126, n.3 (2011). I refer to these below as the three elements. 
16. 
Requirements are recalculated as exposure moves and released as it declines. PFMI Principle 6, 
Key Consideration 4 requires marking positions to market and collecting variation margin “at least 
daily to limit the build-up of current exposures,” together with the authority and operational 
capacity to make intraday calls. PFMI Principle 6, Key Consideration 7 requires that the margin 
system be regularly reviewed and validated. 
17. 
PJM’s own credit policy is constructed on these principles. The general credit requirement is sized 
to Peak Market Activity, computed from a participant’s own observed billing history; unsecured 
credit allowances are keyed to creditworthiness and tangible net worth; and requirements are 
recalculated on an ongoing basis. Attachment Q, Section V.A provides that collateral no longer 
required “shall be returned at the request of a Participant no later than two Business Days” 
following PJMSettlement’s determination; that a Participant may substitute one approved form of 
collateral for another absent a default; and that interest on cash accrues to the benefit of the 
Participant. 
18. 
Where PJM faces forward price exposure, it measures that exposure directly. The FTR Credit 
Requirement is calculated on a portfolio basis as initial margin, less Auction Revenue Right 
Credits, less Mark-to-Auction Value, less realized gains and losses, subject to a floor. Initial 
margin for FTR Obligations is “determined utilizing a historical simulation value-at-risk 
methodology that calculates the size and value at risk of the applicable FTR portfolio,” aggregated 
by straight sum for long-term positions and by a combination of straight sum and weighted root 
sum of squares for balance-of-period positions. The model “will employ a confidence interval of 
99 percent” — the same standard PFMI Principle 6, Key Consideration 3 requires. Historical 
values are adjusted forward where PJM’s economic planning model indicates that transmission 
upgrades will reduce congestion, and PJM may recalculate at any time and must do so no less 
frequently than after each annual FTR auction. 
19. 
For planned resources in the capacity market, PJM sizes the requirement to Net Cost of New Entry 
for the applicable region or Locational Deliverability Area, subject to a floor, and reduces it as 
construction risk is retired. Attachment Q, Section VI.B.3 provides that the RPM Auction Credit 
requirement “shall be reduced” on a stated schedule of five construction milestones, each initiated 
by written request of the Market Participant and supported by defined evidence.

5 
 
20. 
The concern with access is not incidental to the Commission’s regulation of RTOs. It is the reason 
the Commission required them. In Order No. 2000 the Commission codified the minimum 
characteristics and functions an entity must satisfy to be an RTO, with the stated goal of promoting 
“efficiency in wholesale electricity markets” and ensuring “that electricity consumers pay the 
lowest price possible for reliable service.” Regional Transmission Orgs., Order No. 2000, 89 
FERC ¶ 61,285, order on reh’g, Order No. 2000-A, 90 FERC ¶ 61,201 (2000). The rule was 
directed at removing the remaining impediments to competition in wholesale power markets, and 
the Commission grounded it in the observation that efficient and competitive markets develop only 
where participants have confidence that the system is administered fairly. A collateral requirement 
imposed by an RTO is a condition of access to the market that RTO was formed to operate. It is 
measured against that purpose. 
21. 
The Commission has also stated the limiting principle on the other side. In establishing credit 
policy, “the role of an RTO is to balance the competing goals of minimizing risk to non-defaulting 
market participants while, at the same time, ensuring that the credit or collateral requirements are 
not so stringent that they unnecessarily inhibit access to the marketplace.” Sw. Power Pool, Inc., 
126 FERC ¶ 61,153, at P 19 (2009) (citing Sw. Power Pool, Inc., 114 FERC ¶ 61,222, at P 1 
(2006), and Midwest Indep. Transmission Sys. Operator, Inc., 115 FERC ¶ 61,296, at P 16 
(2006)). 
22. 
The Commission has applied that standard to reject a proposed RTO credit provision. In the same 
order it found a revision defining default as occurring upon a missed invoice date, rather than at 
the end of the cure period, “may be so stringent as to unnecessarily inhibit access to the 
marketplace,” and rejected it. Id. at P 21. The Commission did so notwithstanding that the 
provision had emerged from the RTO’s stakeholder process, holding that “the Commission cannot 
accept any proposal from the stakeholder process that is unduly burdensome or unduly 
discriminatory.” Id. The Commission credited the concern that a single default could trigger cross-
default provisions in customers’ other agreements, and placed on the RTO the burden of showing 
that such provisions could be avoided. Id. and n.23. 
23. 
The same standard appears in PFMI Principle 18, which requires “objective, risk-based, and 
publicly disclosed criteria for participation, which permit fair and open access.” 
24. 
A participant must also be able to determine what the requirement will cost it. PFMI Principle 23 
requires that an infrastructure “provide sufficient information to enable participants to have an 
accurate understanding of the risks, fees, and other material costs they incur by participating,” and 
that “all relevant rules and key procedures should be publicly disclosed.” 
25. 
Commercial practice outside the organized markets follows the same architecture — rating-based 
unsecured thresholds, variation margin recalculated as exposure moves, negotiable forms of 
support, and termination payments measured by replacement cost rather than remaining notional. 
26. 
Where a central counterparty intermediates, an uncovered default mutualizes to the membership, 
and the defaulting participant’s own margin absorbs the loss first. PFMI ¶¶ 1.13, 3.4.24. 
PJMSettlement occupies that position in the PJM markets, and Attachment Q, Section I states the 
purpose accordingly: PJM “must have the authority to monitor and manage credit risk on an 
ongoing basis, and to act promptly to mitigate or reduce any unsecured credit risk, in order to 
protect the PJM Markets and PJM Members from losses.” 
IV.  PARTIES AND EXPOSURES UNDER THE RBP 
27. 
This section identifies who bears what under the RBP. That question is prior to any judgment 
about whether the credit requirement is correctly sized, because collateral secures a party against a 
loss, and one cannot evaluate the amount without first knowing whose loss it is and who is 
protected from it. A commercial arrangement of this kind involves four distinct roles: the party 
that posts collateral, the party that pays, the party that receives the benefit, and the party that

6 
 
absorbs a default. In an ordinary bilateral contract these align. Under the proposed provisions they 
do not. I set out the structure here and address its consequences in the opinions that follow. 
A.  Parties with obligations 
28. 
RBP Sellers submit Sell Offers, receive commitments for a fixed fifteen-year term, and post 
collateral under section 18.8(a) equal to 20% of the offer price times committed UCAP MW times 
365 days, for the first three Delivery Years. 
29. 
A seller that fails to achieve commercial operation is subject to RBP shortfall charges under 
section 18.6(d), assessed daily on the full committed UCAP at a rate of 20% of the commitment 
price, for up to three years. A resource delayed solely by Network Upgrades is excepted if it 
demonstrates readiness through test energy and seeks interim deliverability. 
30. 
Under section 18.6(e), if committed MW fail to come online for three Delivery Years the 
commitment is rescinded for the remainder of the fifteen-year term. The resource is then neither 
compensated nor subject to further shortfall charges. Seller exposure is therefore bounded at three 
years of shortfall charges, and the seller’s collateral is sized to that same quantity. That 
administrative cap on the seller’s assessed liability is distinct from the economic replacement 
exposure experienced by load when the capacity does not arrive, which I address at paragraphs 90 
to 95. 
31. 
Load Serving Entities allocated RBP Charges pay the contract-for-differences settlement for the 
full fifteen-year term and post collateral under section 18.8(b) at $1.5 million per RBP UCAP 
MW. Only LSEs in zones with a non-zero Load Adjustment are allocated RBP Charges. 
32. 
PJMSettlement is counterparty to the transactions. 
B.  Parties without obligations 
33. 
Electric Distributors determine the allocation of RBP Obligation MW among LSEs within their 
zone or area. Proposed Reliability Assurance Agreement, section 7.2C. They incur no payment 
obligation and post no collateral. 
C.  The residual tier 
34. 
Under Operating Agreement section 15.2.2, where a Member defaults on its payment obligations 
the other PJM Members may be required to pay a share of the defaulted amounts. That exposure 
extends to Members with no Load Adjustment and no RBP Charge allocation. 
D.  How a default travels 
35. 
On an LSE default, section 18.9(a) provides that the defaulted RBP Charge “will be allocated to 
all remaining Load Serving Entities responsible for paying RBP Charges based on their pro-rata 
share,” and that such amounts “may be offset by the RBP Collateral posted by the defaulting Load 
Serving Entity.” Reallocation is mandatory; application of the defaulter’s collateral is permissive. 
36. 
On a seller default, section 18.9(b) provides that where an RBP Resource defaults on payment of 
shortfall charges, “the corresponding credits will not be allocated to the Load Serving Entities that 
would otherwise receive the RBP shortfall credits.” Load bears the loss directly. 
37. 
The two provisions are asymmetric in effect. A load default is recovered from other load. A seller 
default leaves load uncompensated, and after rescission under section 18.6(e) load receives 
nothing for the remaining twelve years of a fifteen-year commitment. 
38. 
Under section 18.6(f), a commitment follows the resource on a change of ownership and continues 
through the end of the fixed term. The identity and financial condition of the party performing the 
commitment may therefore change during the term while the commitment itself does not. I address 
the treatment of seller credit over the term in Section VII.

7 
 
E.  Which party is harmed by which failure 
39. 
The RBP has three distinct failure modes, and they harm different parties at different times. The 
first is a failure by a Load Serving Entity to post the required collateral on the stated date, which is 
a liquidity event occurring forty-five days before the Delivery Year begins. The second is a failure 
by a Load Serving Entity to pay an RBP Charge, which is a credit event arising during the 
Delivery Year. The third is non-delivery by an RBP Seller, which is a physical event. The first two 
are both financial but are not the same: they are triggered by different conditions, arise on different 
dates, and are secured differently. Collateral secures the second. It does not secure the first, 
because the first is a failure to provide the collateral itself. Collateral is ordinarily sized to the loss 
it prevents, so these distinctions are prior to any judgment about the amount of either requirement. 
40. 
A payment failure by an LSE does not affect whether capacity is delivered. The committed 
resource remains committed and the procurement proceeds. What occurs is a reallocation. Under 
section 18.9(a) the defaulted RBP Charge is allocated among the remaining Load Serving Entities 
responsible for paying RBP Charges; because RBP Charges are assessed against every zone/area 
holding a share of the RBP Target, that population is footprint-wide rather than confined to the 
zone in which the default occurred. Under Operating Agreement section 15.2.2 any residual 
reaches the wider membership. The parties harmed are therefore other load. Within a zone/area, 
the Electric Distributor assigns RBP Obligation MW in the first instance to the Load Serving 
Entities serving the Large Loads whose forecast growth generated the Load Adjustment; where it 
does not, section 18.8(b)(i)(B)(2) reaches load on Peak Load Contribution, which is native load. 
The Large Loads are not themselves parties to the RBP and bear no share of the reallocation under 
section 18.9(a). 
41. 
Non-delivery by an RBP Seller has the opposite incidence. The capacity for which the 
procurement was conducted does not arrive, and the reliability the RBP was designed to secure is 
not obtained. That harm falls on the loads the procurement was designed to serve. PJM has 
described a framework under which RBP supply matched to specific Large Loads would be 
credited as a Bring Your Own Capacity showing for Interim Resource Adequacy Service 
purposes, but the filed provisions establish no mechanism by which an RBP commitment is 
matched to a particular Large Load or Load Serving Entity, and I express no view on how such a 
credit would be determined. The harm falls on load generally, both through the resource adequacy 
shortfall and financially: under section 18.9(b) load does not receive the shortfall credits, and after 
rescission under section 18.6(e) load receives nothing for the remaining twelve years of a fifteen-
year commitment. 
42. 
Neither the tariff nor the filing quantifies the second of those harms. Shortfall charges under 
section 18.6(d) are assessed for up to three years at a rate fixed by reference to the commitment 
price; they are not a measure of the cost of replacing the capacity that did not arrive. PJM 
identified the same gap in its own analysis, stating that a default in year three of a fifteen-year 
contract leaves twelve years of capital cost uncovered, and that the current tariff does not calculate 
liquidated damages. I address the consequences of that gap in Sections VII and IX. 
F.  Application to EKPC 
43. 
PJM’s illustrative allocation shows EKPC with a Load Adjustment of zero and no allocation of the 
RBP Target. EKPC would therefore not be allocated RBP Charges on those figures, and would not 
post RBP Collateral. EKPC nonetheless remains within the residual tier under Operating 
Agreement section 15.2.2. EKPC is the Load Serving Entity for its member-owner distribution 
cooperatives, and an obligation allocated to those cooperatives’ load would be borne by EKPC. 
The quantity that sets each Load Serving Entity’s collateral requirement is submitted by its 
Electric Distributor. That entity incurs no payment obligation, posts no collateral, and need not 
itself be a PJM Member. The party that determines the size of the requirement is therefore not the 
party subject to it, and PJM’s credit provisions reach only the latter.

PART TWO — THE CREDIT REQUIREMENT  
VI.  OPINION 1 — The magnitude has no precedent in PJM 
61. 
This opinion addresses magnitude. The Commission’s standard has two sides: an RTO must 
minimize the risk that a default is socialized among non-defaulting participants, while “ensuring 
that the credit or collateral requirements are not so stringent that they unnecessarily inhibit access 
to the marketplace.” Sw. Power Pool, Inc., 126 FERC ¶ 61,153, at P 19 (2009). Magnitude is the 
measure of the second. In what follows I compare the proposed requirement to the collateral PJM 
actually holds, to the relationship PJM maintains between collateral and market activity, and to the 
annual charge the requirement secures. On each comparison the proposed requirement stands apart 
from anything in PJM’s experience.

10 
 
62. 
At the Initial RBP Target of 6,831.3 UCAP MW, the LSE collateral requirement is approximately 
$10.2 billion. On the illustrative Final RBP Target of 6,075.7 MW it is approximately $9.1 billion. 
PJM’s own illustration of a 100 MW allocation is $150,000,000. Kelly Aff. ¶ 33. 
63. 
PJM’s monthly Key Risk Metrics reporting shows the total collateral PJM holds from all 
Members, against every market it operates, at approximately $6.2 billion on average in 2024 and 
$7.0 billion in 2025. Collateral rose materially in 2026 as measured exposure rose — PJM reports 
that three of the highest billing weeks in its history occurred that year — reaching approximately 
$13.1 billion in February 2026, the highest balance PJM has ever held, and standing at 
approximately $10.9 billion on July 30, 2026. 
64. 
The proposed requirement for a single procurement of 6,831.3 UCAP MW is therefore 
approximately 78% of the largest collateral balance PJM has ever held, and approximately 96% of 
the average balance held during 2026 to date. Against the 2024 and 2025 averages it is 165% and 
146% respectively. 
65. 
Methodology. The series is constructed from PJM’s monthly Key Risk Metrics reporting to the 
Risk Management Committee. Figures are stated as approximate and rounded to the nearest $0.1 
billion. I present them as approximate deliberately. At this magnitude the precision of any single 
month is not material to the conclusion, which rests on the ratio between the collateral PJM holds 
and the market activity that collateral secures. Attachment A. 
66. 
The relationship PJM maintains between collateral and market activity is stable. Measured against 
settlements processed, collateral ran approximately 12% in 2024 and 9% in 2025. Measured 
against the Independent Market Monitor’s total cost of wholesale power, it ran approximately 11% 
in calendar 2025 and 13% over the twelve months ended June 2026. Two differently constructed 
measures place PJM’s collateral coverage in a band of roughly 9% to 13% of annual market 
activity. I use that band below. 
67. 
The requirement is secured at a multiple of the value it secures. At the $555 maximum willingness 
to pay and the Initial RBP Target of 6,831.3 UCAP MW, the maximum gross annual commitment

approximately $573 million. Measured against that amount, the collateral requirement is 
approximately 1,790%. The comparison to PJM's existing markets should be made on a consistent

the requirement with securing a stream that is never billed — the multiple is on the order of fifty-
five to eighty-five times. I use the latter figure below. The comparison is not one of scale alone. 
The collateral PJM holds today secures every market it operates and every class of participant in

The aggregate requirement resolves into zonal allocations of substantial size. On PJM’s illustrative

VII.  WHETHER THE REQUIREMENT SECURES A MEASURED EXPOSURE 
71. 
This section evaluates whether the proposed collateral secures a measured risk position, and 
whether the amount is sufficient or deficient under plausible future price outcomes. The standards 
set out in Section III require that collateral be sized to replacement cost, which is a function of the 
price at which the position would be replaced and the period over which the exposure is held; that 
the requirement be recalculated as exposure moves and released as it declines; and that a 
participant be able to determine what the requirement will cost it. I apply those elements here. 
A.  The requirement is absent during the period of greatest uncertainty 
72. 
Commitments bind when results are posted on December 2, 2026. Buyer collateral is not due until 
forty-five days before the start of the 2028/2029 Delivery Year, approximately April 17, 2028. For 
roughly seventeen months no LSE collateral secures the obligation. The obligation is not merely 
fixed during that period; its first year is already measurable. The 2028/2029 Base Residual 
Auction cleared in July 2026 at $325.00/MW-day, so at the moment the RBP commitment binds 
the first Delivery Year’s contract-for-differences exposure is known at $230/MW-day, or $83,950 
per MW-year. Nor does the position remain single-year for long. The 2029/2030 Base Residual 
Auction results post on December 22, 2026, twenty days after RBP commitments bind, so within 
three weeks two Delivery Years are priced; by the April 2028 posting date they will have been 
known for approximately sixteen months. PJM requires no collateral against a quantified exposure 
for seventeen months, and the requirement it does impose is fixed without reference to prices that 
become observable almost immediately. 
73. 
That interval is when the identity of the obligated party is least certain. RBP Obligation MW are 
reported to PJM by the Electric Distributor. If a large load fails to materialize, or fails to contract 
with a Load Serving Entity, the load on which the obligation was premised does not appear. 
74. 
The tariff allocates that shortfall in two tiers. Under section 18.8(b)(i)(B)(1), RBP Obligation MW

76. 
The RBP settles as a contract for differences. Under section 18.5(g)(ii), an RBP Resource offers 
into RPM as a price taker, clears, and receives the RPM clearing price. The RBP Charge pays the

VIII.  THE QUANTITY OF MW TO WHICH THE CREDIT RATE APPLIES IS 
INDETERMINATE 
99. 
This section addresses the third question posed to me: whether a Load Serving Entity subject to an 
RBP Charge can determine, from the filed rate, the amount it will be required to post. The Credit 
Rate is a price per MW. The amount an LSE must post is therefore the product of that rate and a 
quantity of MW. Section 18.8 specifies three different quantities and does not state which governs 
when they diverge. 
A.  The three quantities 
100. 
The first is committed MW. Section 18.8(b)(i)(A) provides that the cumulative requirement “shall 
be equivalent to the product of the RBP Credit Rate multiplied by RBP UCAP MW committed,”

16 
 
defined as “the amount of RBP UCAP MW that receives a commitment through the Reliability 
Backstop Procurement minus each commitment of RBP UCAP MW that is rescinded pursuant to 
Tariff, Attachment DD, section 18.6(e).” 
101. 
The second is the Final RBP Target. Section 18.8(b)(i)(B)(1) requires each LSE to post “$1.5 
million x the allocated RBP Obligation MW,” where that quantity is “submitted for the Load 
Serving Entity by the Electric Distributor and scaled, as necessary, in the event that the RBP 
Obligation MW values uploaded by the Electric Distributor do not sum to the fixed, Final RBP 
Target MW for the zone/area.” 
102. 
The third is the Daily Unforced Capacity Obligation. Section 18.8(b)(i)(B)(2) provides that where 
no RBP Obligations are reported for a zone, the requirement is based on “the Load Serving 
Entity’s pro-rata share of the Daily Unforced Capacity Obligation for the zone/area as determined 
in RAA, Schedule 8.” That quantity is a function of the LSE’s peak load contribution and bears no 
relationship to the RBP commitment. 
B.  Committed MW and the Final RBP Target will not be the same 
103. 
PJM states expressly that the two will diverge, and in both directions. Section 18.5(f) provides that 
“RBP Resources shall not be partially cleared,” and that “[i]n the event that the Reliability 
Backstop Procurement cannot meet the Final RBP Target, the Reliability Backstop Procurement 
shall clear short of the Final RBP Target.” The same section permits PJM to “commit an RBP Sell 
Offer with an offered quantity that exceeds the remaining Final RBP Target to the extent such 
solution provides greater economic efficiency.” 
104. 
PJM explains the reason: “Because the RBP is procuring new capacity and not simply fungible 
UCAP MW … there exists the possibility that PJM may clear a set of resources with a cumulative 
RBP UCAP MW total that does not exactly match the Final RBP Target.” 
105. 
The divergence is material. On the illustrative Final RBP Target of 6,075.7 UCAP MW, the 
requirement scaled to that target is approximately $9.11 billion. Were the procurement to clear 
five percent short, the requirement computed on committed MW would be approximately $8.66 
billion — a difference of approximately $456 million. Were it to clear five percent over, the 
difference would be the same amount in the opposite direction. Nothing in section 18.8 states 
which figure controls. 
C.  Committed MW is not in-service MW 
106. 
The only reduction to committed MW is rescission under section 18.6(e), which requires that MW 
“fail to come online for three Delivery Years.” Commercial operation dates are permitted as late as 
June 1, 2032, and RBP Sell Offers may be selected for first Delivery Years through 2032/2033. 
Demand Resources and Distributed Energy Resources may also participate, with their own in-
service dates, so the composition of committed MW varies across the term as well as its quantity. 
107. 
A resource committed for a first Delivery Year of 2032/2033 is therefore included in committed 
MW from the 2028/2029 Delivery Year, when it is neither in service nor generating any RBP 
Charge. A resource that fails to appear in 2028/2029 remains in committed MW until rescission 
takes effect after the 2030/2031 Delivery Year. In the first Delivery Year of the term, the quantity 
to which the Credit Rate applies may bear no relationship to the capacity actually delivering or to 
the charges actually billed. 
D.  Consequence 
108. 
An LSE cannot compute the collateral it would be required to post from the tariff. It does not 
know whether the governing quantity is committed MW, the zonal Final RBP Target, or its share 
of the Daily Unforced Capacity Obligation; it does not know the extent to which committed MW 
will exceed or fall short of the Final Target until procurement results are posted; and it cannot 
determine from any of the three what capacity will actually be in service in the Delivery Year for

which it is posting. The standards set out in Section III require that a participant be able to have 
“an accurate understanding of the risks, fees, and other material costs” it incurs. PFMI, Principle 
23.

109. 
This section addresses the release of collateral as exposure declines. The standards set out in 
Section III call for recalculation as exposure moves and release as it declines. For purposes of this

110.

X.  THE COST OF CARRYING THE REQUIREMENT IS MATERIAL AND IS NOT 
RECOVERED 
122. 
This section addresses the cost to a Load Serving Entity of holding the required collateral. That 
cost is not a charge under the tariff and appears in no figure PJM has presented. It is nonetheless a 
real cost, it is borne by load, and it is a direct consequence of the amount and form of collateral 
PJM has proposed. 
123. 
The analysis in this section rests on an assumption that I state expressly. It assumes that the Load 
Serving Entity is able to fund the required amount — from balance sheet cash, from committed 
credit capacity, or by incurring debt — and it measures only the cost of doing so. It does not 
address whether an entity of a given size can obtain funding of the required magnitude at all, and it 
does not attempt to quantify the effect on an entity’s credit standing of assuming an obligation of 
this size. Those questions are distinct from the carrying cost and I address them separately in 
Section XI, where I examine the financial capacity of one investment-grade Load Serving Entity 
against the allocation PJM’s illustrative figures would assign to it. The figures in this section are 
therefore a lower bound: they represent the cost to an entity for which funding is available on the 
terms assumed. 
A.  Only two forms of collateral are permitted 
124. 
RBP Collateral is defined as “either (1) a cash deposit, including any interest thereon, or (2) a 
letter of credit issued for the benefit of PJM or PJMSettlement.” Surety bonds are excluded, 
although PJM accepts them elsewhere subject to per-issuer limits, and section 18.8 provides no 
unsecured credit allowance. An LSE therefore has two options, and the cost of the requirement is 
the cost of whichever it elects. 
B.  Cash 
125. 
An LSE posting cash must fund the amount. The cost is its own cost of funds, less whatever return 
the deposit earns. Attachment Q provides that interest on cash accrues to the benefit of the 
Participant, without specifying a rate. PJM’s audited financial statements for 2025 indicate a 
credited return of approximately 3.8%, below the effective federal funds rate for the same period, 
and interest is credited to a member account periodically rather than continuously. 
126. 
An LSE that posts cash therefore bears the difference between its cost of funds and that credited 
return. For an investment-grade load-serving entity with a cost of funds in the range of 5% to 6% 
— the range addressed at paragraph 130 — the net cost of posting cash is therefore approximately 
120 to 220 basis points on the amount posted. A lower-rated entity would bear a higher cost. I do 
not use the 9.5% after-tax weighted average cost of capital PJM applied in deriving the Credit 
Rate. As explained at paragraphs 129 through 132, that figure describes the cost of capital for 
merchant generation investment, not the cost of funds of the load-serving entities required to post 
the collateral. 
C.  Letter of credit 
127. 
A letter of credit does not require the LSE to fund the amount, but it consumes committed credit 
capacity and is priced accordingly, as a spread over a reference rate together with a facility fee. 
The cost is a function of the issuing bank’s pricing and the borrower’s credit, and the filing places

20 
 
no evidence of either on the record. I therefore state the cost as a range rather than a single figure. 
At 100 basis points the annual cost is approximately $15,000 per RBP UCAP MW; at 200 basis 
points, approximately $30,000; and at 300 basis points, approximately $45,000. A letter of credit 
fee is not the same quantity as a corporate bond yield, and I do not equate them. I use these values 
as sensitivities rather than as estimates of the price any particular load-serving entity would obtain. 
128. 
I do not state a single blended cost across the two forms. PJM presently observes a mix of 
approximately thirty-five percent cash and sixty-five percent letters of credit across its markets, 
but that mix is observed against a total collateral balance that has never exceeded approximately 
$13.1 billion across every market and every participant, and against a period in which PJM's own 
reporting records the extension of unsecured credit alongside it. I do not assume that this historical 
mix would remain unchanged under a single incremental requirement of approximately $10.2 
billion imposed on one class of participants on one date, and I do not rely on it. 
D.  The rate PJM selected is not the rate applicable to load 
129. 
PJM applied a discount rate of 9.5% in deriving the Credit Rate, stating that it “is the capacity 
market Weighted Average Cost of Capital developed by The Brattle Group [ ] as part of PJM’s 
2025 periodic review of the Cost of New Entry of Capacity Resources into the PJM Region.” 
Kelly Aff. ¶ 28. That figure is an after-tax weighted average cost of capital for merchant 
generation investment. It describes the cost of capital of the party selling into the procurement, not 
the party paying for it. The filing offers no rationale for its application to load-serving entities. I 
express no view on whether 9.5% was an appropriate input to PJM’s own valuation exercise. My 
point is narrower: that figure is not evidence of the financing cost a Load Serving Entity incurs to 
post cash or obtain a letter of credit, and the filing offers no other evidence of that cost. 
130. 
PJM has separately represented that approximately seventy-seven percent of load is served by 
investment-grade entities. Published market data establish the cost of funds available to corporate 
borrowers across the rating spectrum, and none of it approaches 9.5% for a population of that 
description. As of August 12, 2026, the ICE BofA index effective yields were: BBB, the lowest 
investment-grade tier, 5.58 percent; BB, the highest non-investment-grade tier, 5.98 percent; 
single-B, 7.25 percent; and CCC and lower, 14.51 percent. PJM’s seventy-seven percent figure is 
load weighted; the entity-count measure PJM presented separately, addressed at paragraph 138 
below, identifies 24 of 105 Load Serving Entities as investment grade. The rating distribution of 
the remainder is not stated, so I present scenarios rather than a single blended figure. A population 
that is seventy-seven percent BBB with the remainder at BB implies approximately 5.67 percent; 
with the remainder at single-B, approximately 5.96 percent; and with the remainder entirely at 
CCC and lower, approximately 7.63 percent. To reach 9.5 percent, approximately forty-four 
percent of the population would have to be rated CCC or below if the remainder were BBB, or 
approximately thirty-one percent if the remainder were single-B. The distribution of those yields is 
itself instructive: the interval between the lowest investment-grade tier and the highest non-
investment-grade tier was forty basis points on that date, and between the highest non-investment-
grade tier and single-B, 127 basis points, while the interval between single-B and CCC and lower 
was 726 basis points. Credit is not priced as a single category above and below the investment-
grade boundary, and the rate PJM selected lies materially above the BBB, BB and single-B index 
yields and below the CCC-and-lower index. Attachment C. 
131. 
This distinction has a further consequence. A predominantly investment-grade population is one to 
which Attachment Q’s unsecured credit allowance would ordinarily extend, keyed to 
creditworthiness and tangible net worth — a mechanism section 18.8 omits entirely. 
E.  In aggregate 
132. 
At the Initial RBP Target, the aggregate annual cost of carrying the requirement ranges from 
approximately $102 million at 100 basis points to approximately $307 million at 300 basis points. 
Measured against the approximately $573 million billed to load in the first Delivery Year, that is

21 
 
between approximately eighteen and fifty-four percent of the amount billed. Each 100 basis points 
on the $1.5 million Credit Rate is $15,000 per MW-year, or approximately $41.10 per MW-day. 
On the sensitivities used above the per-unit cost is approximately $41.10 per MW-day at 100 basis 
points, $61.64 at 150, $82.19 at 200 and $123.29 at 300 — which, measured against the $555 
maximum willingness to pay rather than against the amount billed, is between approximately 
seven and twenty-two percent of that cap, additional to it and recovered nowhere in the proposed 
tariff. The two ranges differ because the denominators differ: the first states carrying cost as a 
proportion of what load is billed, the second as a proportion of the ceiling PJM has represented as 
the limit of what load will pay. The per-MW-day figure does not depend on the size of the 
procurement: because both the collateral and the MW-days scale with committed UCAP MW, the 
quantity cancels. 
F.  The cost is not recovered and is not disclosed 
133. 
No provision of the proposed tariff recovers this cost. It does not appear in the maximum 
willingness to pay, in the RBP Charge, or in any figure PJM has presented to the Commission. A 
Load Serving Entity must either absorb that cost or recover it through its applicable retail or 
contractual arrangements, and where an LSE or the large load it serves fails to appear, the 
requirement is reassigned under section 18.8(b)(i)(B) to the remaining large-load LSEs in the zone 
and, where none remain, to native load. 
134. 
As set out above, the Commission established Regional Transmission Organizations to promote 
efficiency in wholesale electricity markets and to ensure that consumers pay the lowest price 
possible for reliable service, and has held that credit and collateral requirements must not be “so 
stringent that they unnecessarily inhibit access to the marketplace.” PJM has presented the $555 
maximum willingness to pay as the limit of what load will pay under this procurement. On PJM’s 
own figures and the forms of collateral its tariff permits, the cost of carrying the required collateral 
is additional to that limit, and on the sensitivities set out above amounts to approximately $102 
million to $307 million each year, or approximately eighteen to fifty-four percent of the amount 
billed to load in the first Delivery Year. The filing does not identify that cost. The analysis in this 
affidavit indicates that a requirement sized on standard collateral practice would be substantially 
smaller for load-serving entities, and larger for RBP Sellers. 
XI.  THE REQUIREMENT CREATES SYSTEMIC LIQUIDITY RISK AMONG THE ENTITIES 
OBLIGATED TO POST IT 
135. 
This section addresses whether the requirement can be met — in the forms the tariff permits and 
on the date it specifies. I approach that question at two levels. The first is aggregate: whether 
approximately $10.2 billion can be raised at one moment, from one class of participants, in two 
instruments, drawn from a limited group of issuing institutions. The second is particular: whether 
the obligation allocated to a given zone is within the financial capacity of the parties serving it. 
The second question is not incidental to the first. A requirement of this design becomes entity-
specific at the point where the required posting approaches or exceeds the obligor’s available 
liquidity and committed credit capacity, and the tariff performs no test of that at any stage. I use 
the NOVEC zone as the illustration because PJM’s own allocation and the obligated entity’s own 
reported financials are both on the public record. The standard is the one set out in Section III: 
credit requirements must not be so stringent that they unnecessarily inhibit access to the 
marketplace, and the Commission has identified cascading default as the consequence it guards 
against. 
A.  The requirement falls at one moment, in two instruments 
136. 
Section 18.8(b)(i)(B)(1) requires each Load Serving Entity with an RBP Obligation to post forty-
five days before the start of the Delivery Year. Every obligated LSE across the footprint posts on 
the same date; nothing in section 18.8 staggers the requirement, phases it, or permits it to be 
sequenced. RBP Collateral is defined as either a cash deposit or a letter of credit. Surety bonds are

22 
 
excluded, although PJM accepts them elsewhere and held approximately $606 million of them on 
July 30, 2026. No unsecured credit allowance is provided and no corporate guaranty is permitted. 
Approximately $10.2 billion therefore becomes due at a single moment, from a single class of 
participants, in two instruments. 
B.  The obligation is concentrated and is not adjusted for the financial capacity of the obligor 
137. 
As set out in Attachment B, five zones each carry an obligation exceeding $1 billion — AEPOHIO 
at approximately $2.29 billion, NVEC at $1.95 billion, COMED at $1.33 billion, PPL at $1.23 
billion and DOM at $1.11 billion — together approximately $7.9 billion, or 77 percent of the 
initial requirement. Each zone’s share is determined by the Electric Distributor’s submission of 
RBP Obligation MW, scaled as necessary to the fixed zonal target. Nothing in that derivation 
refers to the financial capacity of the entity required to post, and nothing in section 18.8 tests it at 
any stage. 
138. 
PJM has measured the credit quality of the population required to post. In the Credit and 
Securitization Overview presented on March 4, 2026, PJM identified 105 Load Serving Entities, 
of which 24 were investment grade and 81 were sub-investment grade. It reported that 46 percent 
had tangible net worth below $5 million and 30 percent below $1 million, that these figures 
indicated “limited financial flexibility,” and that investment-grade entities had “provided corporate 
guarantees.” PJM therefore had a measurement of the financial capacity of the obligated 
population before the requirement was filed. 
139. 
For scale, $10.2 billion is equivalent to approximately $97.6 million for each of the 105 Load

report tangible net worth below $5 million. The actual requirement is not distributed evenly; it is 
concentrated among the Load Serving Entities that receive RBP obligations. The allocation to the 
NOVEC zone alone is approximately nineteen percent of the entire initial requirement and 
approximately twenty times the average share, and it falls on a single distribution cooperative.

D.  Letter of credit capacity is concentrated 
145. 
As of July 30, 2026 PJM held approximately $6.87 billion in letters of credit issued by 43 
institutions, of which the ten largest accounted for approximately 65 percent of the total and two 
individually exceeded 10 percent. PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Credit Risk Metrics, Risk 
Management Committee, at slide 4 (Aug. 18, 2026).4 Satisfying the RBP requirement 
predominantly by letter of credit would more than double the letter of credit exposure PJM holds, 
drawn from substantially the same group of institutions. 
146. 
PJM monitors and reports monthly on the letters of credit posted by issuing banks. That reporting 
includes the concentration by volume among the largest issuers. It is provided to keep Members 
informed of how PJM is managing the credit risk it holds through third parties. PJM has broad 
discretion to decline a letter of credit from a bank on concentration grounds. The membership 
prudently supported that discretion in the comprehensive credit policy overhaul PJM filed in 2020, 
because it allows PJM to manage not only a Member’s direct credit risk but also the manner in 
which the Member chooses to mitigate the risk it presents to the broader membership. No analysis 
appears on the record addressing whether the RBP requirement can be satisfied without creating 
concentration risk among the banks that would issue the letters of credit. PJM measures that 
concentration every month because it bears directly on the quality of the collateral PJM holds. The 
filed requirement would roughly double the letter of credit portfolio, drawn from substantially the 
same institutions, and the filing does not measure it at all. 
E.  The failure mode is correlated, and PJM has handled the same structure differently 
147. 
The exposures created by the requirement are correlated rather than independent. All obligated 
Load Serving Entities post on the same date, in the same two instruments, drawn from the same 
limited group of issuing institutions, against an obligation whose quantity a Load Serving Entity 
has only limited means to affect. The assignment is made by the Electric Distributor under 
proposed Reliability Assurance Agreement, section 7.2C, and may be reassigned by it; and the 
procurement target itself may be reduced before the procurement closes on evidence of the kind 
PJM identified during the stakeholder process. Neither is a means by which a Load Serving Entity 
holding an assigned obligation can reduce that obligation once the commitment binds, which is the 
period during which the collateral is required. Under section 18.9(a), a default is reallocated pro

148. 
PJM has faced a structurally comparable situation. Following Winter Storm Elliott, PJM assessed

PJM did not demand the full amount at a single moment. It sought authority to extend the period

150. 
Section 18.8 contains no equivalent. It states a date and an amount. It provides no phase-in, no

unable to satisfy the requirement on the stated date may propose an alternative. The consequence

provision does, not because supplying that discretion would answer the questions addressed in this

population on which it lands. 
F.  Conclusion 
151. 
In my opinion the filing does not establish that the proposed requirement can be met by the 
population required to post it. It does not analyze the aggregate letter of credit capacity available to 
the obligated population, the effect of a simultaneous call on entities that cannot reduce their 
exposure by managing their positions, or the consequences in any zone where the obligation 
exceeds the financial capacity of the parties serving it. The NOVEC zone shows that the question 
is not hypothetical: an obligation of approximately $1.95 billion is allocated to a footprint served 
by a cooperative reporting approximately $1.716 billion in total assets, whose customers have no 
general right to select an alternative Load Serving Entity that would bear the cost and collateral 
exposure in its place. 
152. 
Where an obligation of that kind cannot be met, the proposed provisions do not extinguish it. 
Section 18.9(a) reallocates the defaulted charge pro rata to the remaining Load Serving Entities, 
and Operating Agreement section 15.2.2 extends what remains to Members with no allocation at 
all. The same features that make the requirement difficult to satisfy — its concentration, its single

where the loss travels when it is not satisfied. That is the subject of the following section.

XII.  THE SOCIALIZATION OF A DEFAULT INCREASES THE OBLIGATION OF THE 
REMAINING LSEs AND REACHES MEMBERS WITH NO ALLOCATION 
153. 
This section addresses where a loss goes. The Commission has identified the prevention of 
socialization as the function collateral performs: where collateral posted by a defaulting party is 
insufficient, the remaining exposure and costs are socialized across the membership. The standards 
set out in Section III order those two things — the defaulting participant’s own margin absorbs the 
loss first, and mutualization is what remains after it is exhausted. Section 18.9(a) does not 
expressly establish that sequence. The proposed provisions also contain two distinct reallocation 
mechanisms, operating on different triggers and different scopes, and the tariff does not 
distinguish them. 
A.  Section 18.9(a) does not expressly require collateral to be applied before reallocation 
154. 
Section 18.9(a) provides that a defaulted RBP Charge “will be allocated to all remaining Load 
Serving Entities responsible for paying RBP Charges based on their pro-rata share,” and that such 
amounts “may be offset by the RBP Collateral posted by the defaulting Load Serving Entity.” 
Reallocation to non-defaulting parties is stated as mandatory. Application of the defaulting party’s 
own collateral is stated as permissive. 
155. 
That differs from the sequence the standards describe and from the sequence PJM applies 
elsewhere. Under Attachment Q, collateral posted against an obligation is applied to that 
obligation upon default, and mutualization under Operating Agreement, section 15.2.2 is the 
residual. Section 18.8 collects $1.5 million per MW from load, and section 18.9(a) does not 
commit PJM to apply it to the loss against which it was collected. 
156. 
I do not suggest that PJM would decline to apply the collateral. The point is that the tariff does not 
require it. The collateral posting is mandatory, while section 18.9(a) states its application to a 
defaulted RBP Charge in permissive terms. If PJM intends that the collateral be applied first, the 
filed text does not state it. 
B.  Two reallocation mechanisms of different scope 
157. 
The proposed provisions reallocate an obligation in two circumstances, and the scope differs. 
Where a large load does not materialize or ceases operation, the obligation is reassigned within the 
zone. Where an allocated Load Serving Entity fails to pay, section 18.9(a) reallocates the defaulted 
charge to “all remaining Load Serving Entities responsible for paying RBP Charges,” language 
that on its face reaches the entire footprint rather than the zone. The tariff does not state that the 
two operate on different scopes, and nothing in section 18.9 confines the payment-default 
reallocation to the zone in which the default occurs. 
C.  Where the load does not appear, the obligation reaches native load 
158. 
PJM described the treatment of a load that does not appear during the stakeholder process. In 
materials presented to the Reliability Backstop Critical Issue Fast Path on June 10–11, 2026, PJM 
stated that where a load does not materialize or shuts down before the end of the RBP term, the 
corresponding large load obligation must be reassigned, and identified three options: the Electric 
Distributor may assign the obligation to another Load Serving Entity; if it does not, and other Load 
Serving Entities in the zone/area hold assignments, the obligation is allocated pro rata among those 
remaining entities by zonal share; and if the Electric Distributor makes no assignments in the 
zone/area, “the costs will be reallocated across all load in the zone on a pro rata basis using the 
Obligation Peak Load Contribution MW (the same methodology used to allocate RPM costs).” 
Design Presentation,  at slide 30. PJM stated in the same materials that if states have not 
established frameworks to allocate costs to new data center loads, “it is unclear to which 
customers those costs would be assigned,” and that as a backstop PJM will allocate to all load in 
the zone, “including non-large loads,” using existing Peak Load Contribution assignments. Id. at 
slide 27. PJM’s stakeholder materials refer to the quantity assigned to a Load Serving Entity as the

27 
 
Large Load Contribution or “LLC” Obligation MW; the PJM Board’s July 27, 2026 decisional 
letter refers to the same quantity as the Reliability Backstop Obligation or “RBO,” described there 
as a new defined term exclusively for the RBP; and the proposed tariff language refers to it as the 
RBP Obligation MW submitted for a Load Serving Entity by the Electric Distributor. The quantity 
is the same in each. I use the tariff term. 
159. 
The filed tariff assigns the allocation function to the Electric Distributor and specifies the outcome 
where it is not performed. Section 18.8(b)(i)(B)(1) provides that the RBP Obligation MW values 
uploaded by the Electric Distributor are “scaled, as necessary, in the event that the RBP Obligation 
MW values uploaded by the Electric Distributor do not sum to the fixed, Final RBP Target MW 
for the zone/area.” Because the zonal quantity is fixed, an obligation not reported for one Load 
Serving Entity is not extinguished; it is scaled onto the others. Section 18.8(b)(i)(B)(2) addresses a 
Load Serving Entity for which the Electric Distributor reports no obligation at all, providing that 
such an entity “may be required to post” collateral determined by its “pro-rata share of the Daily 
Unforced Capacity Obligation for the zone/area as determined in RAA, Schedule 8” — that is, on 
Peak Load Contribution. Section 18.3(a) fixes the zonal allocation for the full fifteen-year term. 
160. 
The structure is a two-step one: the Electric Distributor assigns, and where it does not, the cost 
falls on all load in the zone/area on Peak Load Contribution. PJM has described the assignment 
step as similar to the existing Peak Load Contribution and Network Service Peak Load processes, 
and Electric Distributors perform an analogous function today. The difference lies in what is 
assigned. Those processes allocate charges that follow measured load: if the load falls, the 
allocated quantity falls with it. The RBP Obligation MW allocates a fixed quantity for fifteen 
years, set on a forecast, which does not decline if the forecast load does not appear. The tariff 
states no standard governing how the Electric Distributor is to make the assignment, and no 
mechanism by which a Load Serving Entity may determine in advance whether it will hold one. 
What the tariff does specify is where the quantity comes to rest if the assignment is not made: on 
all load in the zone/area, including load that is not large load. In the NVEC zone/area the two steps 
reach the same entity. Northern Virginia Electric Cooperative performs the assignment as Electric 
Distributor and is the Load Serving Entity on which the cost falls if it does not, and there is no 
other Load Serving Entity in that zone/area to which the obligation could be assigned. 
161. 
The quantities that fix each zone’s share were not prepared for this purpose. The Load 
Adjustments underlying the RBP Target derive from large load additions reported through PJM’s 
load forecasting process and taken from Table B-9b of the 2026 Load Forecast, as the difference 
between forecast summer 2028 and summer 2026 peak load. Those submissions were made to 
inform a planning forecast. They carried no cost consequence for the submitting entity, and were 
not accompanied by verification procedures directed to their use in allocating a fifteen-year 
payment and collateral obligation. Section 18.3(a) then fixes the resulting allocation for the full 
fifteen-year term on that single vintage. 
D.  The NOVEC zone 
162. 
The consequence is measurable, and its distribution across customer classes is not uniform. As set 
out in the preceding section, the NOVEC zone carries an initial allocation of 1,302.6 UCAP MW 
and a collateral obligation of approximately $1.95 billion. Northern Virginia Electric Cooperative 
serves that zone and reports energy sales of approximately 14.649 billion kilowatt-hours for the
