a system load factor of approximately 71 percent. That system figure conceals two classes with 
materially different characteristics. The cooperative reports that data centers represent more than 
65 percent of its energy sales. I use 65 percent in the calculations that follow, which is therefore a 
lower bound. Data center load typically operates at a load factor of 85 to 95 percent; residential 
and small commercial load operates at approximately 40 to 55 percent, and load factors for the 
residential class are observable from default service and basic generation service supply auctions. 
The conclusion does not depend on the precise figures. What the difference in load factor

28 
 
establishes is that a charge collected on peak load contribution rather than on energy falls on the 
two classes in materially different proportion to the energy each consumes, and that the direction 
of the disparity is against the class that consumes less. Selecting the low end of the data center 
range and the high end of the residential range understates that disparity, and I do so below. 
163. 
That difference matters because RBP Charges are allocated on a demand basis rather than an 
energy basis. Where obligations are not assigned to the Large Loads that produced them, the 
quantity falls to Peak Load Contribution — the Obligation Peak Load Contribution MW that PJM 
states is “the same methodology used to allocate RPM costs.” The two classes therefore bear the 
obligation in proportion to their contribution to peak, not to their consumption of energy. On the 
load factors stated above, non-data-center load accounts for approximately 35 percent of energy 
but approximately 45 to 53 percent of peak load contribution. 
164. 
The effect is to shift the burden toward the lower-load-factor class. At the 2028/2029 Base 
Residual Auction clearing price of $325.00/MW-day and an RBP price of $555, the contract-for-
differences differential is $230/MW-day, or $83,950 per MW-year, and the first-year charge 
allocated to the zone is approximately $109 million. Allocated on peak load contribution, that 
charge falls at approximately $11.63 to $13.62 per megawatt-hour on non-data-center load, against 
approximately $6.45 to $7.53 per megawatt-hour on the data center load whose forecast growth 
produced the allocation. The uniform energy-basis figure, approximately $8.96 per megawatt-
hour, understates the former and overstates the latter. The conclusion does not depend on the 
particular load factors selected; it holds across the full range set out in Attachment D. 
165. 
The cost of carrying the collateral is allocated the same way and compounds the same disparity. At 
150 basis points — a midpoint of the sensitivity range set out in Section X, stated here for 
illustration — the annual carrying cost for the zone is approximately $29 million, of which 
approximately $14 million falls on non-data-center load — approximately $3.38 per megawatt-
hour, against approximately $1.88 per megawatt-hour for data centers. Taken together, the charge 
and the cost of the collateral securing it fall at approximately $16 per megawatt-hour, or 1.6 cents 
per kilowatt-hour, on native load, against approximately $8.88 per megawatt-hour on data centers. 
The cooperative reports a monthly average residential cost of $113.74 for 1,000 kilowatt-hours; 
the incremental burden on that bill is approximately fourteen percent. These figures are borne by 
the customers of a distribution cooperative reporting total assets of approximately $1.716 billion 
and patronage capital and margins of approximately $44.7 million, who have no general right to 
purchase generation from a competitive supplier. I do not suggest that outcome is the expected 
one. I state it because the tariff makes it available, because it arises under the allocation 
methodology PJM itself specifies, and because PJM has acknowledged that it does not know to 
which customers the costs would be assigned. Passing the cost through does not resolve the matter. 
Whether the cooperative assigns it to the Large Loads it serves or recovers it from native load, the 
allocation from PJM is unchanged. Those loads did not face a charge of this kind before the RBP 
was proposed, and a cost of this magnitude may bear on whether a given development proceeds. If 
it does not proceed, the allocation does not follow it: the RBP Obligation MW for the zone/area is 
fixed under section 18.3(a) for the full fifteen-year term on the basis of the load forecast used to 
set it, and it is not revised if the forecast load does not materialize. The cooperative would remain 
responsible for an allocation calculated on load that did not arrive. The cooperative was in any 
event already before its state commission on the question of assigning large-load costs: on July 17, 
2026 it announced a filing to update the rate classes applicable to large-load customers so that 
costs attributable to serving those customers are assigned to them rather than shifted to smaller 
users, with a further step to follow involving updated load forecasts and a power supply 
solicitation. 
E.  The NOVEC zone does not satisfy the conditions for the opt-out 
166. 
PJM identified this problem during the stakeholder process and included an opt-out addressing that 
concern. Explaining the opt-out at section 18.1(d), PJM states that cooperatives raised the concern

29 
 
that an Electric Distributor in a retail choice state, not regulated by the state and not otherwise 
serving as the LSE for generation to the load, “would be forced to have its customers absorb the 
costs of an ‘overbuy’ if a particular large load included in the forecast were to fail to materialize,” 
and that unlike a state-regulated investor-owned utility, cooperatives and municipal utilities “are 
not governed by a state regulatory authority that would be responsible for addressing the potential 
reallocation of RBP costs.” PJM describes this as a limited regulatory gap faced by cooperatives 
and municipal utilities “whose rates are not regulated by the states.” 
167. 
The opt-out is available only on that condition. The retail rates of Virginia distribution 
cooperatives are regulated by the Virginia State Corporation Commission. A distribution 
cooperative is a utility consumer services cooperative under Chapter 9.1 of Title 56 of the Code of 
Virginia, and its regulated utility services are subject to the jurisdiction of the Commission in the 
same manner and to the same extent as those provided by other persons under the laws of the 
Commonwealth. Va. Code §§ 56-231.33, 56-231.34; see also Va. Code § 56-585.3; 20 Va. Admin. 
Code § 5-200-21 (rules governing streamlined and general rate proceedings for electric 
cooperatives subject to the Commission’s rate jurisdiction). Each of the cooperative’s filed rate 
schedules provides that service is available “subject to the Terms and Conditions of the 
Cooperative filed with the State Corporation Commission of Virginia.” Northern Virginia Electric 
Cooperative, Schedule HV-2, Large Power Dedicated Facilities Contract Service, Regulated 
Rates. The cooperative states on the same basis that the Commission “approves rates, fees and all 
terms and conditions of service of the Cooperative.” The cooperative serving the NOVEC zone is 
therefore ineligible for the opt-out, notwithstanding that it faces precisely the exposure PJM 
described: an obligation fixed for fifteen years on a forecast of large load additions, which under 
section 18.8(b)(i)(B)(2) reaches its native load if that load does not materialize. The zone carrying 
the second largest allocation in the procurement, and the only zone in which the obligation 
exceeds the reported assets of the entity serving it, cannot use the remedy PJM built for the 
problem PJM identified. 
F.  The residual reaches Members with no allocation 
168. 
Operating Agreement, section 15.2.2 provides that where a Member defaults on its payment 
obligations, the other PJM Members may be required to pay a share of the defaulted amounts. That 
provision is not limited to Members allocated RBP Charges. 
169. 
East Kentucky Power Cooperative is in that position. PJM’s illustrative allocation shows EKPC 
with a Load Adjustment of zero and no allocation of the RBP Target. On those figures EKPC 
would be allocated no RBP Charges and would post no RBP Collateral. It nonetheless remains a 
PJM Member and remains within the residual tier. The assessment under section 15.2.2 is made to 
EKPC as the PJM Member. 
170. 
A Member in that position receives no capacity from the procurement, pays no RBP Charge, and 
posts no collateral, yet bears exposure to a default under it. No collateral is posted against that 
exposure by any party, because the requirement in section 18.8 reaches only Load Serving Entities 
with an allocated obligation. I do not suggest that a Member in EKPC’s position should be 
required to post collateral. The observation is that the requirement PJM has designed does not 
reach the exposure such a Member bears. 
G.  The seller side runs the same direction 
171. 
Section 18.9(b) provides that where an RBP Resource defaults on payment of shortfall charges, 
“the corresponding credits will not be allocated to the Load Serving Entities that would otherwise 
receive the RBP shortfall credits.” There is no reallocation among sellers and no provision 
applying the seller’s collateral to make load whole. 
172. 
The seller’s assessed liability is limited to the three-year shortfall period, while the economic 
consequence to load can continue after the commitment is rescinded. Under section 18.6(e), a 
commitment that fails to come online for three Delivery Years is rescinded for the remainder of

30 
 
the term; the resource is thereafter neither compensated nor charged, and its collateral is released. 
Load receives nothing for the remaining twelve years of a fifteen-year commitment. 
173. 
The two provisions produce the same result from opposite facts. A load default is recovered from 
other load. A seller default is also borne by load. Under the two default paths identified in the 
filing, any unrecovered loss ultimately reaches load or the residual PJM membership. 
H.  Conclusion 
174. 
In my opinion the proposed provisions do not prevent the socialization of a default. They establish 
the paths by which residual losses are reallocated. The collateral posting is mandatory, while 
section 18.9(a) states its application to a defaulted RBP Charge in permissive terms. Where 
forecast Large Load does not materialize, the obligation remains within the zone and, under the 
final allocation step PJM describes, may ultimately be allocated to native load by Peak Load 
Contribution. An LSE payment default is addressed separately under section 18.9(a), which 
reallocates the defaulted charge among all remaining Load Serving Entities responsible for paying 
RBP Charges. Because RBP Charges are assessed against every zone/area holding a share of the 
RBP Target, that reallocation reaches the footprint and is not confined to the zone in which the 
default occurs. The remedy PJM designed for the cooperative overbuy problem is conditioned so 
as to exclude cooperatives whose rates are state-regulated. And the residual extends to Members 
who take nothing from the procurement and post nothing against it. 
XIII.  THE FILED CREDIT CONSTRUCTS WERE NOT EXAMINED IN THEIR FINAL FORM 
175. 
This section addresses the process by which the credit provisions developed. I raise it because 
credit and collateral were material design issues throughout the stakeholder process, because 
materially different approaches were proposed by PJM and other stakeholders, and because the 
methodologies ultimately filed were not examined in their final form. The Commission has held 
that credit requirements emerging from an RTO stakeholder process must still be reviewed for 
whether they are unduly burdensome. Sw. Power Pool, Inc., 126 FERC ¶ 61,153, at PP 20-21 
(2009). The relevant question for my analysis is what opportunity existed for stakeholders to 
examine the magnitude, mechanics and liquidity consequences of the credit requirements 
ultimately proposed. 
A.  PJM proposed using its existing credit framework for LSEs 
176. 
PJM addressed LSE credit requirements in its stakeholder materials on at least two occasions. In 
the Design Presentation, PJM stated that upon notification by the Load Serving Entity of known 
changes to its load, “the credit, and collateral requirements for LSEs are expected to be managed 
by the current credit processes,” and that those processes “include, but are not limited to, credit 
evaluation, peak market activity (PMA) recalculation and use of other mitigation tools, such as 
posting of credit support and/or unreasonable credit risk collateral calls (UCRs).” The same 
language appears in PJM’s Stage 4 proposal paper of June 30, 2026. 
177. 
That was a description of PJM’s existing credit framework applied to a new charge. It contained 
no fixed rate per megawatt, no aggregate requirement, no single posting date, and no stated 
departure from Peak Market Activity. As discussed above, Peak Market Activity based on 
historical billing would not by itself have captured the prospective exposure created by a new 
fifteen-year RBP obligation, and that limitation was raised during the stakeholder process. But the 
approach PJM described retained the principal elements of its existing credit framework: credit 
evaluation, recalculation of expected exposure through PMA, and the use of additional mitigation 
tools where the calculated exposure was not adequately secured. Nothing in the June 10–11 or 
June 30 materials identified a Credit Rate of $1.5 million per RBP UCAP MW or an aggregate 
LSE collateral requirement of approximately $10.2 billion.

31 
 
B.  Other stakeholder proposals addressed buyer credit differently 
178. 
Credit and collateral were not absent from the stakeholder debate. Other proposals addressed the 
issue directly and proposed materially different approaches. The Joint EDC and Data Center 
Coalition proposal, which ultimately received the greatest sector-weighted support, tied 
procurement to the ability of the subscribing LSE or Large Load to satisfy the applicable credit 
requirement at the time PJM committed supply resources. An LSE unable to satisfy that 
requirement could not subscribe MW into the procurement. The Joint Consumer Advocates 
likewise identified credit and collateral as an issue in the procurement. 
179. 
The Coalition described the objective of its credit methodology in exposure terms. It proposed a 
requirement intended to ensure that “any emerging buyer default exposure is recognized early, 
funded continuously, and contained entirely within the LSE buyer” that subscribed to or received 
the RBP obligation. It also contemplated that the credit requirement would attach when the RBP 
commitment was made and “adjust[] over time.” That approach therefore contemplated both 
measurement of emerging exposure and adjustment of the requirement as that exposure changed. 
180. 
The Joint Consumer Advocates likewise identified demand-side credit and collateral as a 
necessary element of the RBP design, but proposed a different structure. Their June 30 executive 
summary stated that demand-side credit and collateral “should be established before 
procurement,” rather than assigned later. Their final recommendations to the Board again called 
for PJM to “[e]stablish demand-side credit and collateral prior to procurement.” They recorded 
PJM staff’s position on that issue as “collateral timing/assignment is later,” and identified as a 
source of stranded cost risk the absence of any opportunity to require Large Loads to commit to 
pay their RBP obligations and to post collateral with the Electric Distributor. Joint Consumer 
Advocates, Stage 4 of PJM CIFP Stakeholder Process Regarding Large Load Additions and 
Reliability Backstop Procurement and Connect & Manage, Executive Summary to the PJM Board 
of Managers (June 30, 2026), at 2, 4, 5. 
181. 
The significance of these proposals for my analysis is not that the Commission should have 
preferred one stakeholder proposal over another. It is that the stakeholder process had identified 
buyer credit as a material RBP design issue and produced materially different approaches to 
addressing it. PJM proposed use of its existing credit framework, including credit evaluation and 
recalculation of exposure. The Coalition proposed that emerging buyer-default exposure be 
recognized early, funded continuously and contained within the subscribing buyer, with the 
requirement adjusting over time. The Joint Consumer Advocates proposed establishing demand-
side collateral before procurement. None of those approaches proposed the fixed $1.5 million per 
MW requirement ultimately filed. 
C.  The seller requirement was materially revised in the final stakeholder proposal 
182. 
Seller credit was also changing late in the process. In the June 10–11 Design Presentation, PJM 
proposed seller credit equal to Max($20, 0.2 × bid price) × MW UCAP committed × 365 × a year 
multiplier, defined as the ratio of the net present value of the multi-year penalty cash flow to the 
nominal value of one year. PJM stated that a fifteen-year tenor at a 9.5% discount rate “equates to 
~seven years.” Its worked example applied a multiplier of 7.31, producing approximately $21.4 
million for a 100 MW commitment at $400/MW-day, or approximately $214,000 per MW. 
183. 
PJM materially revised that construct in its final June 30 proposal. The Stage 4 proposal paper 
states the seller requirement as “Max ($20, 0.2 x bid/clearing price) x MW UCAP committed x 
365 x 3 (years),” and explains that PJM was “proposing to require credit support equivalent to 
three years of the RBP shortfall charges.” Compared on a common basis, at the maximum 
willingness to pay of $555/MW-day the June 10–11 formulation with its 7.31 multiplier produces 
approximately $296,166 per MW, while the June 30 formulation produces $121,545 per MW — a 
reduction of approximately 59 percent. Section 18.8(a) as filed adopts the June 30 formulation 
without further change.

32 
 
184. 
The timing is relevant. The material revision to seller credit was disclosed in PJM’s final June 30 
stakeholder proposal, after which no further stakeholder meetings were held. Stakeholders 
therefore received the revised seller methodology before the filing, but had no subsequent 
stakeholder meeting at which to examine it. The RBP proposal was filed on July 31, 2026, thirty-
one days after the final stakeholder proposal. 
D.  The LSE requirement changed after the final stakeholder proposal 
185. 
The treatment of LSE credit followed a different sequence. PJM’s final June 30 proposal 
continued to state that LSE credit and collateral requirements were expected to be managed 
through existing credit processes, including credit evaluation, Peak Market Activity recalculation 
and other mitigation tools. The fixed $1.5 million per RBP UCAP MW requirement does not 
appear in those materials. 
186. 
The July 31 filing replaced that approach. Section 18.8(b) establishes a fixed Credit Rate of $1.5 
million per RBP UCAP MW, which PJM derived from approximately fifty percent of the gross 
fifteen-year contractual value. At the Initial RBP Target, that produces an aggregate LSE collateral 
requirement of approximately $10.2 billion. The methodology therefore first appeared after the 
final stakeholder proposal and in the filing itself. 
187. 
The change was not an increase in the amount of collateral produced by the methodology 
presented to stakeholders. The filed construct instead departed from the criteria PJM had identified 
for determining LSE credit under its existing process. The $1.5 million per MW Credit Rate does 
not depend on the credit quality of the LSE, a recalculation of Peak Market Activity or expected 
exposure, or the use of other mitigation tools to address an identified deficiency. It applies the 
same fixed rate per megawatt before unsecured credit to every LSE subject to section 18.8(b), 
regardless of those considerations. 
188. 
Both credit constructs were therefore moving late in the process, as were other elements of the 
proposal. The Joint Consumer Advocates recorded that PJM staff had revised substantial elements 
of the Reliability Backstop Procurement and Connect and Manage proposals at least three times in 
the month preceding June 30, 2026, including on the evening before the original deadline for 
stakeholders to submit their own Stage 4 proposals. Id. at 2 n.6. The material change to seller 
credit was disclosed in PJM’s final June 30 proposal, but there was no subsequent stakeholder 
meeting at which it could be examined. The material change to LSE credit occurred after that final 
proposal and first appeared in the July 31 filing. At the same time, the stakeholder process had 
produced other approaches to buyer credit that were substantively different from both PJM’s June 
30 approach and the methodology ultimately filed. Neither filed construct therefore received 
stakeholder examination in its final form, and the specific $1.5 million per MW LSE methodology 
was not presented for stakeholder examination before the filing. 
E.  The filed methodologies departed from the exposure-based criteria considered during the process 
189. 
The sequence is relevant to the substance of the methodologies ultimately filed. The approaches 
presented during the stakeholder process differed in important respects, but collectively they 
reflected several criteria ordinarily associated with managing credit exposure, and PJM’s own 
analysis presented to the process applied those criteria directly. PJM’s June 30 proposal retained 
credit evaluation, PMA recalculation and additional mitigation tools. The Coalition proposal 
expressly called for emerging buyer-default exposure to be recognized early, funded continuously 
and contained within the responsible buyer, with the requirement adjusting over time. The Joint 
Consumer Advocates emphasized establishing the credit and collateral requirement before the 
procurement occurred. 
190. 
PJM also presented an exposure-based analysis of the construct to the stakeholder process. In the 
March 4 Credit Overview, PJM stated that the Reliability Back-Stop Auction “introduces 15-year 
contractual durations, which current PJM credit rules were not designed to mitigate,” and that 
Attachment Q “is primarily built for short-term settlement cycle and one-year capacity

33 
 
obligations.” It identified the resulting vulnerability as a “liquidity squeeze,” comprising a “sizable 
collateral requirement,” constraints on liquidity, and “cost of capital.” It also stated that “[c]urrent 
tariff does not calculate liquidated damages.” 
191. 
That presentation modeled the procurement as a fixed-for-float swap and estimated potential 
future exposure across the fifteen-year term. PJM defined potential future exposure as the 
maximum exposure of economic value to a counterparty at a future point in time, at a stated 
confidence level such as 95 percent. PJM did not present a flat profile. The estimate begins at zero, 
rises through the early Delivery Years, reaches a maximum within roughly the first third of the 
term, and declines to zero at expiry. PJM stated the reason: “The value uncertainty goes higher 
deeper into the future, while quantity exposure decreases as time goes by. This makes PFE peaks 
at 1/3 of life.” PJM’s estimate is denominated in millions of dollars per MW, and at no point 
across the fifteen-year term does the exposure PJM depicted reach $1.2 million per MW. By 
contrast, section 18.8 establishes a fixed $1.5 million per MW Credit Rate rather than a 
requirement that follows that modeled exposure profile. The filed requirement therefore exceeds 
the maximum exposure PJM itself modeled at every point in the term, and exceeds it by a wide 
margin in the opening and closing years, when PJM’s own estimate approaches zero. PJM had 
before the stakeholder process an estimate of buyer-side exposure that varies across the term and 
amortizes to zero. 
192. 
The same presentation set out the credit profile of the population that would be required to post. 
As described at ¶ 138 above, PJM identified 105 Load Serving Entities, of which 24 were 
investment grade and 81 sub-investment grade, with 46 percent below $5 million in tangible net 
worth and 30 percent below $1 million, and noted that investment-grade LSEs had “provided 
corporate guarantees.” PJM therefore also had before the process a measurement of the credit 
quality of the entities on which the requirement would fall, and of the mitigation already in place. 
193. 
Section 18.8(b) as filed adopts none of those criteria for determining the initial LSE requirement. 
It does not measure the LSE’s expected RBP settlement exposure; it does not establish the initial 
requirement through Peak Market Activity or another exposure calculation; it does not vary the 
Credit Rate according to participant credit quality; and it does not establish a methodology for 
determining when additional or alternative mitigation is required. Instead, the initial requirement is 
determined by multiplying a fixed $1.5 million Credit Rate by the applicable quantity of RBP 
UCAP MW. Nor does the filed construct reflect the exposure profile PJM itself modeled, or the 
credit quality PJM itself measured. Potential future exposure as PJM estimated it rises and then 
declines to zero across the term; the Credit Rate is a single figure that does not decline at all. And 
the same $1.5 million per MW Credit Rate applies to each Load Serving Entity that receives an 
RBP obligation, without regard to the credit classification PJM assigned to that entity. 
F.  PJM considered adjustment mechanisms for sellers that were not included for load 
194. 
The June Design Presentation also demonstrates that PJM considered mechanisms for adjusting 
seller collateral over the term. It presented a year-by-year seller credit requirement schedule, 
including a column labeled “RBP Credit Req. Desired (NPV),” defined as “collateral required if 
the NPV is recalculated through out the contract term,” declining from approximately $21.4 
million to $819,568 for the 100 MW commitment used in the example — approximately $214,000 
to $8,196 per MW. PJM stated that the step down in collateral would be “contingent on credit 
valuation per Att. Q,” and that the credit requirement “may be reduced to reflect the remaining 
years while taking into account the credit quality of the Market Participant.” 
195. 
PJM therefore considered for sellers both periodic recalculation of the remaining obligation and 
adjustment for participant credit quality. Neither mechanism appears in the filed LSE construct. 
Section 18.8(b) provides no schedule for recalculation, no defined reduction methodology, and no 
unsecured credit allowance keyed to creditworthiness. As discussed in Section IX, it provides only 
that the Credit Rate “may be reduced” by the Office of the Interconnection over time.

34 
 
G.  PJM states that the filed proposal was not stakeholder-endorsed 
196. 
PJM describes the status of the proposal expressly. Distinguishing NRG Power Marketing, LLC v. 
FERC in its transmittal, PJM states that “the proposal submitted in this filing was authorized by 
the PJM Board and was not the result of a stakeholder-endorsed proposal.” 
197. 
The absence of stakeholder endorsement does not itself determine whether a credit requirement is 
reasonable. The Commission has rejected a credit provision that had been developed through an 
RTO stakeholder process and approved by its Board, holding that it “cannot accept any proposal 
from the stakeholder process that is unduly burdensome or unduly discriminatory.” Sw. Power 
Pool, Inc., 126 FERC ¶ 61,153, at PP 20-21 (2009) (quoting Sw. Power Pool, Inc., 114 FERC ¶ 
61,222, at P 19 (2006)). The Commission rejected the provision as “not consistent with or superior 
to the pro forma OATT” and as potentially “so stringent as to unnecessarily inhibit access to the 
marketplace,” notwithstanding that the revisions were the product of the SPP stakeholder process 
and had been approved by the SPP Board of Directors. Id. The relevance of the process here is 
narrower. Stakeholder review provides an opportunity for the entities subject to a credit 
requirement to identify its operational, financing and liquidity consequences and to test the 
methodology used to measure the exposure before it is implemented. 
H.  Conclusion 
198. 
In my opinion, neither of the credit constructs ultimately filed received stakeholder examination in 
its final form. Seller credit was materially revised in PJM’s final June 30 proposal, after which no 
further stakeholder meetings were held. The fixed $1.5 million per MW LSE requirement was not 
included in that final proposal and first appeared in the July 31 filing. 
199. 
This is significant because the stakeholder process had not ignored credit risk. PJM and other 
stakeholders had proposed different means of addressing it. Those approaches included credit 
evaluation, recalculation or continuing measurement of exposure, adjustment of the requirement 
over time, additional mitigation when needed, and establishment of buyer credit before 
procurement. The filed LSE methodology did not select among those approaches. It instead 
established a fixed Credit Rate derived from the gross contractual value and omitted the exposure-
based criteria that had been identified during the stakeholder process. 
200. 
For a credit construct of this magnitude, those differences are material. The stakeholder process 
provided no opportunity to examine the $1.5 million per MW methodology against the matters 
addressed in this affidavit: its relationship to measured exposure; the quantity to which the Credit 
Rate applies; the availability and cost of permitted collateral; the mechanism by which collateral is 
reduced as exposure declines; the financial capacity of the entities required to post it; the 
consequences of a simultaneous collateral call; and the allocation of loss following default. The 
filed $1.5 million per MW methodology therefore was not subjected to stakeholder examination 
against those considerations before the filing. 
XIV.  CONCLUSION 
201. 
I believe the matters set out above point to a straightforward characterization of what section 18.8 
does. PJM took the gross contractual value of a fifteen-year commitment, halved it, and called the 
result collateral. Nearly every difficulty addressed in this affidavit follows from that single step. 
202. 
Collateral, as PJM administers it everywhere else in its markets, requires three things: an identified 
position that would have to be replaced on default, a price at which it would be replaced, and a 
period over which the exposure is held before replacement is complete. Attachment Q is built on 
those elements. RPM auction credit, FTR credit and Peak Market Activity are each measured 
against them, recalculated as conditions change, and released as the exposure declines. Section 
18.8 identifies none of the three. It states a rate and a date.

35 
 
203. 
The seller requirement confirms the diagnosis rather than qualifying it. Both sides of the RBP face 
the same quantity and the same two prices. The obligation is denominated in the same RBP UCAP 
MW, and the amount that moves between them in any Delivery Year is the difference between the 
RBP price and the RPM clearing price for that year. The economic consequence being analyzed on 
each side therefore depends on the same two prices and the same committed quantity. Symmetry 
in the exposure does not produce symmetry in the collateral. Section 18.8(a) requires a seller to 
post approximately $121,545 per MW, while section 18.8(b) requires load to post $1.5 million per 
MW against the same quantity and the same prices — roughly twelve times as much. Measured 
against the two Delivery Years whose differential is known within twenty days of commitment, 
the seller posts less than the exposure and load posts about nine times it. As set out in Section VII, 
the two requirements also imply contradictory RPM price paths: the seller figure is adequate only 
if RPM clears at or above approximately $532.80/MW-day on average, and above approximately 
$564.12 across the thirteen years that remain unpriced, while the load figure corresponds to the 
exposure only if RPM clears at or below approximately $281.03. No single price path satisfies 
both. Two requirements derived from one measured exposure would not diverge in this way. 
These did not begin from one. 
204. 
The timing of the load requirement is the clearest demonstration that it is not calibrated to 
exposure. Commitments bind when results post on December 2, 2026. The 2028/2029 Base 
Residual Auction has already cleared at $325.00/MW-day, so the first Delivery Year's exposure is 
known at the moment the commitment binds. The 2029/2030 results post on December 22, 2026, 
twenty days later. Within three weeks of commitment, therefore, two Delivery Years are priced, 
and on the adjusted target of approximately 6,000 MW the exposure they represent is 
approximately $1.0 billion, taking the 2029/2030 year at the $333.44 proxy discussed above. 
Against that quantified exposure PJM requires no collateral at all for approximately seventeen 
months, until roughly April 17, 2028. It instead requires approximately $9.1 billion on the same 
target against an exposure it has never quantified, beginning at the point when a substantial part of 
the position has become knowable and is no longer in doubt. A requirement that is absent where 
the exposure is measurable and largest where it is unmeasured is not a risk instrument. 
205. 
The remaining difficulties are consequences rather than independent defects. Because the 
requirement is not tied to a measured exposure, there is no quantity against which to apply it, and 
the tariff supplies three that do not agree. Because the filed methodology does not measure the 
exposure, it provides no exposure-based basis for reducing the requirement as that exposure 
declines, and section 18.8(b)(i)(A) provides only that the Credit Rate “may be reduced.” Because 
the amount is not sized to a risk, the cost of carrying it — approximately $102 million to $307 
million a year against approximately $573 million billed to load in the first Delivery Year — 
appears in no figure PJM has presented and is recovered by no provision of the tariff. And because 
it falls on a single date, in two instruments, drawn from the same limited group of issuing 
institutions, without regard to the balance sheet of the entity obligated to post, it creates the 
correlated exposure that a credit policy exists to prevent. 
206. 
The point I made at the outset holds at the end of it. A security deposit is sized to the damage a 
tenant might do, not to the rent due over the life of the lease. A landlord who demanded six 
months’ rent on a twelve-month lease would be asked what damage he expected, and would be 
expected to answer. PJM has not identified the damage. 
207. 
None of this suggests that the RBP requires no credit support. It plainly does. Section 18.9(a) 
socializes a defaulted RBP Charge pro rata across the remaining Load Serving Entities, and under 
Operating Agreement, section 15.2.2 the residual reaches Members holding no allocation at all. A 
requirement set too low leaves native load bearing the cost of another party’s default. That is the 
harm collateral exists to prevent, and it is the harm the Commission identified in the Policy 
Statement on Electric Creditworthiness as the function of collateral to avoid.

36 
 
208. 
But the error runs in both directions, and that is what makes the matter difficult rather than simple. 
A requirement set too high inhibits access to the market the RTO was formed to operate, and 
where it is large enough relative to the balance sheets on which it falls, it creates the systemic 
exposure it was meant to prevent. The Commission has held that “the role of an RTO is to balance 
the competing goals of minimizing risk to non-defaulting market participants while, at the same 
time, ensuring that the credit or collateral requirements are not so stringent that they unnecessarily 
inhibit access to the marketplace,” and has rejected a credit provision on that ground 
notwithstanding that it emerged from an RTO stakeholder process and was approved by that 
RTO’s board. Sw. Power Pool, Inc., 126 FERC ¶ 61,153, at PP 19, 21 (2009). The NOVEC zone 
illustrates that the second error is not hypothetical here: an allocation of approximately $1.95 
billion falls on a distribution cooperative reporting total assets of approximately $1.716 billion and 
cash and temporary investments of approximately $243.2 million. 
209. 
That two-sided character bears directly on what can be done with the filing. The appropriate 
requirement cannot be determined from the filed formula alone. It requires the exposure to be 
measured — the position, the replacement price, the close-out horizon — and it requires the 
resulting number to be tested against the financial capacity of the entities that would post it. That 
second step cannot be performed on this record. The balance sheets of the obligated Load Serving 
Entities are not before the Commission. Neither is the letter of credit capacity available to them, 
the cost at which they could raise cash, or the effect of a simultaneous call on their existing 
facilities. Those are the facts on which any sound construct depends, and they reside with the 
parties rather than with PJM or the Commission. 
210. 
The stakeholder process ordinarily provides an opportunity for that examination. As set out in 
Section XIII, credit and collateral were considered during that process, but the specific $1.5 
million per MW methodology first appeared in the July 31 filing and therefore was not subjected 
to stakeholder examination before filing. It was not tested there against the elements set out in 
Section III, against the quantity to which it applies, against the cost of the permitted forms of 
collateral, or against the capacity of the entities on which it falls. In my opinion the deficiency in 
the filed construct is not a matter of calibration that could be corrected by adjusting the rate. It is 
that the analysis on which any rate would rest was not performed, and the present record does not 
contain the participant-specific financial and liquidity information needed to perform it.
